summary: This WebMD health guide, medically reviewed by Mahammad Juber, MD on September 20, 2022, describes asparagus as a springtime vegetable and outlines its health benefits. It covers vitamins and fiber supporting eyes, blood clotting, antioxidant defense, digestion, heart health and prenatal health. It also lists nutrients per half-cup serving and gives common ways to prepare asparagus.
one_line: WebMD guide to asparagus covering its health benefits, nutrition per serving, and preparation methods.
key_facts: The name asparagus comes from the Greek word "asparagos," which means "to spring up."
Asparagus was first found in the Mediterranean thousands of years ago.
Vitamin A is important for keeping eyes healthy and helps prevent cataracts or macular degeneration.
Vitamin K helps blood clot properly, and a deficiency can lead to uncontrolled bleeding after an injury.
People taking blood thinning medications like warfarin should watch their Vitamin K intake and check with a doctor.
Free radicals are oxygen particles that cells produce as waste and can damage cell DNA, leading to cancer or heart disease.
Dietary fiber fuels good bacteria that help the body digest food and absorb nutrients.
A single serving of asparagus provides a third of the folic acid the average person needs daily.
One half-cup serving of asparagus (about 4 spears) contains 13 calories, 1 gram of protein, 2 grams of carbohydrates and 1 gram of fiber.
Asparagus is a good source of Vitamins A, C, E and K, folate and potassium.
Asparagus is in season in early spring, from March to May.
Asparagus is best eaten cooked; boiling, steaming, frying and grilling are common cooking methods.
Cooked asparagus is commonly served with hollandaise sauce.
Insoluble fiber in asparagus binds to cholesterol in the digestive system and helps carry it out before absorption.
Folate is critical during early pregnancy because it helps the baby's organs form correctly and prevents brain and spine birth defects.
